title: Bictegravir/TAF/FTC: One-Tablet HIV Therapy With Interaction Checks
bottomLine: Bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide is a complete antiretroviral regimen for HIV-1 in appropriate patients. Adherence and interaction review are essential, and stopping the tenofovir/emtricitabine components in a patient with hepatitis B can trigger a serious HBV flare.
recognize: Antacids/mineral supplements can interact with integrase inhibitors depending on product and timing.
Renal, hepatic, and hepatitis B status affect safe regimen selection and monitoring.
priorities: Verify the complete ART regimen, adherence, renal/hepatic context, HBV status, and interacting medications/supplements.
Escalate jaundice, severe renal deterioration, lactic-acidosis symptoms, or suspected treatment failure.
assessMonitor: Trend viral-load/CD4 results as ordered, renal/hepatic status, adherence, and drug interactions.
interventions: Administer consistently and reinforce that missed doses can contribute to virologic failure/resistance.
medicationSafety: Do not add duplicate antiretroviral components without prescriber/pharmacist review.
Current labeling carries a boxed warning for post-treatment acute exacerbation of hepatitis B.
teaching: Take ART consistently, disclose all supplements/antacids, and never stop the regimen abruptly without HIV-team guidance.
delegationScope: Routine medication administration and adherence reinforcement may be within PN scope; regimen selection and treatment-failure evaluation require HIV-specialist/provider collaboration.
examTrap: Stopping Biktarvy abruptly in a patient with chronic hepatitis B because HIV viral load is suppressed.
oneLinePearl: ART works when the whole regimen is taken consistently—and HBV makes stopping risky.
sourceBasis: NIH Adult and Adolescent ART Guidelines current 2026

title: Dolutegravir: Integrase Inhibition and Mineral Interactions
bottomLine: Dolutegravir is an integrase strand transfer inhibitor used with other antiretrovirals for HIV treatment and in selected PEP regimens. The major nursing safety themes are adherence, polyvalent-cation interactions, hypersensitivity/hepatic reactions, and avoiding accidental incomplete ART.
recognize: Iron, calcium, magnesium, and aluminum products can alter dolutegravir absorption depending on food/timing.
Rash plus systemic illness or liver injury can signal a serious hypersensitivity reaction.
priorities: Review the complete ART regimen, antacids/mineral supplements, liver disease/HBV-HCV coinfection, and adherence.
Escalate severe rash, fever/systemic symptoms, or hepatic-injury findings.
assessMonitor: Trend viral response, liver-related symptoms/labs when ordered, adherence, and medication interactions.
interventions: Use current product-specific instructions for spacing or coadministration with polyvalent cations.
medicationSafety: Dolutegravir should not be treated as monotherapy for established HIV infection.
Review dofetilide and other important interaction contraindications in the current label.
teaching: Take exactly as prescribed and check before starting new antacids, mineral supplements, or interacting drugs.
delegationScope: Administration/reinforcement may be within PN scope; regimen design and serious toxicity evaluation require provider/pharmacist collaboration.
examTrap: Giving dolutegravir with an interacting mineral product without checking timing instructions.
oneLinePearl: Dolutegravir is potent—but minerals and incomplete regimens can undermine it.
sourceBasis: NIH Adult and Adolescent ART Guidelines current 2026

title: Oral HIV PrEP: Kidney, HBV, and Adherence Safety
bottomLine: Daily oral emtricitabine/tenofovir-based PrEP is highly effective HIV prevention when taken as prescribed. Safe use requires confirming HIV-negative status, assessing kidney function, checking hepatitis B status, supporting adherence, and repeating HIV testing on schedule.
recognize: Oral tenofovir can affect kidney function in some patients.
Stopping FTC/tenofovir in a patient with active hepatitis B can allow HBV rebound and liver injury.
priorities: Verify current HIV testing, renal function, HBV screening, medication list, and adherence barriers.
Escalate suspected acute HIV infection, significant renal decline, or hepatic flare after discontinuation.
assessMonitor: Trend HIV testing, kidney function at guideline-defined intervals, STI screening, adherence, and HBV follow-up when relevant.
interventions: Reinforce daily adherence and comprehensive STI/pregnancy prevention counseling based on patient goals.
medicationSafety: PrEP is for patients without HIV; using a two-drug PrEP regimen in undiagnosed HIV can promote resistance.
Current CDC guidance distinguishes renal eligibility for F/TDF versus F/TAF.
complications: Drug resistance if HIV is unrecognized
redFlags: Fever/rash/sore throat after recent HIV exposure
teaching: PrEP prevents HIV but not other STIs or pregnancy; regular testing remains part of treatment.
delegationScope: Education reinforcement and ordered monitoring may be within PN scope; PrEP prescribing/eligibility decisions remain provider responsibilities.
examTrap: Starting or continuing two-drug oral PrEP without resolving symptoms that could represent acute HIV infection.
oneLinePearl: PrEP safety starts with a negative HIV test, kidneys, HBV, and adherence.
sourceBasis: CDC Clinical Guidance for PrEP updated 2026-04

title: Injectable Cabotegravir PrEP: Testing and the Long Tail
bottomLine: Long-acting injectable cabotegravir is an HIV PrEP option that avoids daily pills but requires reliable injection follow-up and repeated HIV testing. Drug levels persist for months after stopping, creating a long pharmacokinetic tail during which inadequate HIV prevention can foster infection and resistance.
recognize: Injection-site reactions are common.
Late or missed injections can reduce protection and require a bridging/restart plan.
priorities: Verify HIV-negative status before injections and assess for symptoms of acute HIV infection.
Track injection schedule and missed-dose plans.
Escalate suspected HIV seroconversion or serious hypersensitivity/hepatic symptoms.
assessMonitor: Trend HIV testing, injection-site reactions, adherence to scheduled visits, and transition coverage if injections stop.
interventions: Use the current injection protocol and ensure follow-up is scheduled before the patient leaves.
medicationSafety: Do not administer PrEP cabotegravir to a patient with confirmed HIV without a complete ART regimen.
The long tail requires ongoing prevention planning after discontinuation.
teaching: Keep every injection/test appointment and use the planned alternative prevention strategy if injections are stopped or delayed.
delegationScope: Administration authority depends on facility/state policy and competency; HIV-status interpretation and PrEP prescribing remain provider responsibilities.
examTrap: Treating a missed long-acting PrEP injection as harmless because medication is still detectable in the body.
oneLinePearl: Long-acting PrEP has a long tail—testing and follow-up protect against resistance.
sourceBasis: CDC Clinical Guidance for PrEP updated 2026-04

title: HIV nPEP: Start Fast, Finish the 28-Day Plan
bottomLine: HIV nonoccupational PEP is time-sensitive prevention after a substantial-risk exposure. CDC recommends initiation as soon as possible and no later than 72 hours, with a 28-day regimen when indicated; do not delay the first dose for nonessential testing when PEP is clearly warranted.
recognize: Current preferred adult/adolescent regimens use bictegravir/FTC/TAF or dolutegravir plus two NRTIs in appropriate patients.
Renal/hepatic disease, pregnancy, drug interactions, and prior long-acting ARV exposure can change regimen choice.
priorities: Identify exposure timing and substantial-risk features immediately.
Obtain baseline testing without delaying indicated treatment.
Support adherence for the full course and arrange follow-up HIV testing.
assessMonitor: Trend medication tolerance/adherence, renal/hepatic status as appropriate, HIV testing, STI/hepatitis needs, and psychosocial safety after assault or other traumatic exposure.
interventions: Administer the prescribed first dose promptly and coordinate follow-up/refill access.
medicationSafety: PEP regimen selection must account for organ function and interactions.
Stop nPEP if expert/provider evaluation later confirms the source does not have HIV and treatment is no longer indicated.
complications: Resistance if HIV infection is already present
teaching: PEP is an emergency medication course, not a one-time dose; complete follow-up testing and discuss transition to PrEP if ongoing risk exists.
delegationScope: The PN can recognize urgency and implement ordered therapy; determining indication/regimen requires authorized provider/expert guidance.
examTrap: Waiting for every baseline lab result before giving the first indicated PEP dose.
oneLinePearl: For PEP, the clock matters: start as soon as possible, then support all 28 days.

title: Combined Hormonal Contraception: Estrogen Changes the Risk Screen
bottomLine: Combined pills, patch, and ring contain estrogen plus progestin. Safe use depends on screening for thrombotic/cardiovascular and migraine risk, measuring blood pressure, reviewing smoking and medication interactions, and teaching that these methods do not prevent STIs.
recognize: Migraine with aura, major thrombotic history, selected severe hypertension, and some smoking/age combinations can make estrogen-containing contraception unsafe under U.S. MEC criteria.
Leg swelling, chest pain, focal neurologic symptoms, or severe new headache require urgent evaluation.
priorities: Confirm BP and screen key U.S. MEC contraindications/precautions before initiation or continuation concerns.
Assess adherence and interacting enzyme-inducing medications.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, new migraine/aura, thrombotic symptoms, bleeding pattern, and adherence.
interventions: Reinforce missed-dose instructions for the exact product and backup contraception when indicated.
medicationSafety: Estrogen-containing contraception is not interchangeable with progestin-only methods for risk assessment.
Hormonal contraception does not protect against STIs/HIV.
teaching: Know the product-specific missed-dose plan and seek urgent care for clot/stroke symptoms.
delegationScope: PNs may reinforce prescribed contraceptive teaching; eligibility/prescribing decisions depend on authorized clinician scope and state law.
examTrap: Treating every hormonal contraceptive as having the same thrombotic risk profile.
oneLinePearl: When estrogen is present, screen pressure, clot risk, migraine aura, and smoking history.

title: Depot Medroxyprogesterone: Long-Acting Progestin and Bone Safety
bottomLine: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate is a long-acting progestin contraceptive. Current U.S. labeling carries a boxed warning for loss of bone mineral density; also expect possible irregular bleeding, weight change, delayed return to fertility, and the need for timely repeat injections.
recognize: DMPA does not contain estrogen, so its eligibility profile differs from combined hormonal contraception.
Bone-health risk matters especially when other osteoporosis risks are present.
priorities: Confirm timing/pregnancy-exclusion criteria per current practice guidance and review bone-health risks, bleeding expectations, and follow-up schedule.
assessMonitor: Trend bleeding pattern, weight, mood concerns, injection schedule, and bone-risk context.
interventions: Administer via the correct IM or SC product/technique when authorized; self-administered SC DMPA is an option under current U.S. guidance for appropriate patients.
medicationSafety: Do not confuse IM and SC products/doses/routes.
DMPA does not protect against STIs/HIV.
complications: Unintended pregnancy if repeat injection is missed
teaching: Keep repeat-injection appointments and discuss calcium/vitamin D, exercise, smoking, and other bone-health risks as appropriate.
delegationScope: Injection administration authority varies by state/facility; contraceptive eligibility and prescribing require authorized clinician scope.
examTrap: Teaching that fertility returns immediately when the last DMPA injection wears off.
oneLinePearl: DMPA is convenient and estrogen-free—but timing and bone health still matter.
sourceBasis: DailyMed medroxyprogesterone acetate injectable labeling updated 2026-02

title: Progestin-Only Pills: Timing and Formulation Matter
bottomLine: Progestin-only pills avoid estrogen-related risk but have formulation-specific timing and missed-pill rules. Safe teaching requires identifying the exact product, checking drug interactions and pregnancy possibility, and explaining expected irregular bleeding.
recognize: Norethindrone/norgestrel and drospirenone progestin-only pills do not share identical missed-dose windows/instructions.
Enzyme-inducing drugs can reduce contraceptive effectiveness for some hormonal methods.
priorities: Identify the exact pill formulation before giving missed-dose advice.
Review adherence, interacting medications, bleeding pattern, and pregnancy concerns.
assessMonitor: Trend adherence, bleeding pattern, side effects, and potassium-related risk when relevant to drospirenone-containing products.
interventions: Use current CDC/product-specific instructions for initiation, missed pills, and backup contraception.
medicationSafety: Do not apply combined-pill missed-dose rules automatically to progestin-only pills.
These pills do not protect against STIs/HIV.
complications: Hyperkalemia risk with selected drospirenone regimens in susceptible patients
redFlags: Severe abdominal pain with positive pregnancy test/ectopic concern
Severe hyperkalemia symptoms in high-risk context
teaching: Take the pill consistently and keep the product-specific missed-dose instructions available.
delegationScope: Teaching reinforcement may be within PN scope; prescribing/eligibility decisions require authorized clinician scope.
examTrap: Giving the same missed-pill advice for every progestin-only pill formulation.
oneLinePearl: With progestin-only pills, know the exact pill before teaching the clock.

title: Levonorgestrel Emergency Contraception: Earlier Is Better
bottomLine: Levonorgestrel emergency contraception reduces pregnancy risk after unprotected intercourse or contraceptive failure and should be taken as soon as possible. It does not terminate an established pregnancy, does not protect against STIs, and effectiveness can be reduced by some enzyme-inducing medications.
recognize: Nausea, abdominal discomfort, fatigue, headache, or menstrual timing changes may occur.
Rifampin, efavirenz, and some antiseizure drugs can reduce levonorgestrel exposure.
priorities: Clarify timing of exposure, current contraceptive method, interacting medications, and whether sexual-assault/STI/HIV PEP needs are present.
Escalate severe abdominal pain or pregnancy concern after use.
assessMonitor: Assess subsequent menses/pregnancy testing needs and ongoing contraception plan.
interventions: Administer/provide as soon as possible according to the product and current U.S. emergency-contraception guidance.
medicationSafety: Do not use as routine contraception when a more reliable ongoing method is desired.
It does not protect against HIV/STIs.
complications: Delayed recognition of ectopic pregnancy if pregnancy occurs
redFlags: Signs of sexual-assault injury or acute HIV/STI exposure needing additional care
teaching: Emergency contraception is time-sensitive; discuss an ongoing contraceptive plan and STI/HIV prevention as appropriate.
delegationScope: OTC access exists for levonorgestrel EC; clinical counseling/prescribing responsibilities vary by setting and state.
examTrap: Telling the patient that levonorgestrel emergency contraception causes abortion or protects against STIs.
oneLinePearl: Levonorgestrel EC works before pregnancy is established—give it early and plan what comes next.
sourceBasis: DailyMed levonorgestrel emergency contraceptive labeling updated 2026-05

title: Ulipristal Emergency Contraception: Five-Day Window, Delay Hormones
bottomLine: Ulipristal acetate is a progesterone-receptor modulator used for emergency contraception within 120 hours after unprotected intercourse or contraceptive failure. Hormonal contraception should generally not be started or resumed until at least 5 days after ulipristal because progestins can reduce its effect.
recognize: Ulipristal remains effective later in the 5-day emergency-contraception window than levonorgestrel in comparative evidence.
Restarting hormonal contraception too soon is a key interaction trap.
priorities: Clarify exposure timing, current hormonal method, interacting medications, pregnancy possibility, and STI/HIV needs.
Provide the exact follow-up plan for restarting contraception and barrier use.
assessMonitor: Assess menstrual follow-up, pregnancy testing if no expected bleed occurs, and ongoing contraception plan.
interventions: Administer as soon as possible within the approved window and follow current CDC guidance for restarting hormonal contraception.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. label/CDC guidance advises delaying hormonal contraception for 5 days after ulipristal.
Strong CYP3A4 inducers can reduce ulipristal effectiveness.
complications: Reduced efficacy from premature progestin restart or enzyme induction
Delayed ectopic-pregnancy recognition if pregnancy occurs
redFlags: Sexual-assault or HIV-exposure needs requiring urgent parallel care
teaching: Wait the recommended interval before restarting hormonal contraception and use barrier protection as instructed afterward.
delegationScope: Administration/counseling roles vary by state and setting; prescribing remains within authorized clinician scope.
examTrap: Restarting a progestin-containing contraceptive the same day as ulipristal.
oneLinePearl: Ulipristal buys a five-day EC window—but progestin has to wait five days too.
